info.title: LANcast HTTP API
info.summary: The contract third-party clients build against.
info.description:
The machine-readable half of the LANcast contract. `docs/api.md` remains the narrative companion and explains *why* each endpoint behaves as it does; this file is what tooling reads.

Authored as JSON rather than YAML on purpose: Go's standard library parses JSON and has no YAML parser, and `internal/api/openapi_test.go` checks this document against the router on every `go test ./...`. Adding a YAML dependency to a repository that hand-rolled an EXIF reader to avoid one was the wrong trade. The cost is that JSON has no comments — which is fine, because prose belongs in `description` fields, where `openapi-typescript` carries it out to JSDoc on the generated client types. A comment would have been lost; a description is delivered.

`/api` is permanently version 1 (ADR 0018). Additive changes ship at any time, so **clients must ignore unknown response fields** and **must tolerate unknown `kind`, `match_state` and error `code` values**. Enum-typed strings in this document are therefore documented as open sets: they list what the server emits today, not what it may emit tomorrow.

Times are Unix seconds. Durations and positions are milliseconds.

servers.description: Relative to the server's own origin. An unsecured server binds 127.0.0.1 only; TLS turns on when the socket reaches beyond this machine (ADR 0014).

get.summary: Liveness, application version, and contract revision
get.description:
One of the five endpoints that does not require a session.

`version` is the application release, stamped from the release tag at build time (ADR 0016); a build from source reports `dev`. `api_version` is the HTTP contract revision and changes only when a new `/api/vN` prefix ships.

200.description: The server is up.

get.summary: What the client should render: setup, login, or the library
get.description:
Does not require a session, and answers differently depending on whether one is present.

This is the one response every screen already fetches, which is why several unrelated facts are reported here rather than from an endpoint of their own.

200.description: Always. An unauthenticated caller gets the same shape without `user`.

post.summary: Create the first administrator
post.description: Only while the server is unconfigured; once an account exists this answers `409 conflict`. Issues a session cookie on success.

200.description: The administrator was created and this caller is now signed in as them.

409.description: An account already exists, so there is no first administrator to create.

post.summary: Exchange a username and password for a session
post.description: Throttled per client IP. **A wrong username and a wrong password are reported identically** as `401 unauthorized`, deliberately: distinguishing them tells an attacker which half they got right.

200.description: Signed in. The session cookie is set on this response.

401.description: Incorrect username or password — the two are not distinguished.

409.description: No accounts exist yet; the caller wants `/auth/setup`.

429.description: Too many attempts from this client; wait a few minutes.

post.summary: End this session only
post.description: Ends the calling session and no other. Contrast `/auth/password`, which revokes every session this account holds.

200.description: The session is gone and the cookie has been cleared.

post.summary: Change your own password
post.description: Changes the calling account's password and **revokes every session that account holds, including this one**. That is the point of server-side sessions, not a bug to smooth over — a client must expect the next request to be answered `401` and send the user back to the login screen.

200.description: Changed. Every session for this account, including the caller's, is now invalid.

get.summary: This server's own cryptographic identity
get.description: Who this server is when it talks to another one (ADR 0044). `fingerprint_display` is the same value grouped for a human to read aloud or compare by eye.

200.description: This server's identity.

get.summary: Every library on this server

200.description: All libraries, with their counts and last-scan verdict.

post.summary: Create a library
post.description:
Administrators only.

`roots` is the multi-location form (ADR 0034). `path` remains accepted and means exactly the same as a single-element `roots` array, so every client that predates multi-root libraries keeps working unchanged. Send one or the other.

409.description: A library already covers that path.

patch.summary: Rename a library, move it, or change its kind
patch.description: Administrators only. Every field is optional; an omitted field is left alone, which is why they are nullable pointers on the server rather than plain strings.

200.description: The library as it now stands.

delete.summary: Delete a library and its rows
delete.description: Administrators only. Removes the library's **records**. It does not touch the media on disk — the server never owns the files.

200.description: Deleted.

get.summary: The locations this library's files live in

200.description: Every root, each carrying the number of rows that would go with it if it were removed.

post.summary: Add a location to this library
post.description: Administrators only.

409.description: That path is already covered by a library.

patch.description: Administrators only. Used when a drive letter changes or a share moves.

200.description: The root as it now stands.

delete.summary: Remove a location from this library
delete.description: Administrators only. Removes the rows that came from that location; the files are untouched.

200.description: Removed.

get.summary: The browse grid: filtered, sorted, paged media
get.description:
**By default the listing is top-level only** — rows with no parent. Children (seasons, episodes, and the `part`/`chapter` pieces of a multi-part work) have a parent and are reached through `parent_id`, never returned loose in the grid, so a container's pieces do not appear as if they were features (ADR 0010, ADR 0017). Passing an explicit `kind` lifts that default.

**A collection is listed only when it groups at least two present members.** A provider supplies a franchise even when the library holds a single film from it, and a collection of one is just a duplicate tile of that film with a "Play all" button. That rule applies to every listing, not only the top-level grid — it was once a property of the grid alone, which made `kind=collection` the one listing that showed the singletons everything else refused. Fetching a collection's own members with `collection_id` is unaffected: the rule hides a collection from listings *of* collections, never what is inside one.

parameters.name: library_id
parameters.description: Restrict to one library.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Free text over title and series, case-insensitive substring. **`library_id` is optional alongside this** — omitting it searches every library, which is what the client's global search does. A search that made you name the library first would ask you to know where a thing is before looking for it.

parameters.name: initial
parameters.description:
The A–Z rail: one letter, or `#` for titles starting with anything that is not a Latin letter. Matches on the item's sort title, case-insensitively.

A **filter, not a scroll offset** — the grid pages in as you scroll, so "jump to S" cannot mean "scroll to a row that has not loaded". `GET /api/libraries/{id}/facets` returns the letters actually present, so a client never offers one that finds nothing.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description:
Restrict to one kind. Passing this also **lifts the top-level-only default**, for a deliberate cross-cutting query such as every episode.

**An open set** (ADR 0018). `movie`, `episode`, `show`, `season`, `serial`, `part`, `chapter`, `collection`, `artist`, `album`, `track`, `gallery`, `photo`, `playlist` and `other` today. New kinds arrive without a major version, so a client with an exhaustive switch is relying on a guarantee this contract does not give.

parameters.name: exclude_kind
parameters.description: Drop kinds from the listing, **comma-separated**. The browse grid passes `collection,playlist`: both group items rather than being them, and a tile beside its own members made a curated shelf read as an unsorted one. Each has its own page. A single value still means what it always did.

parameters.name: parent_id
parameters.description: Return the children of one item — a show's episodes, a work's parts.

parameters.name: collection_id
parameters.description: Return a collection's members. Membership is many-to-many and is **not** `parent_id`, which is always empty for a collection (ADR 0017).

parameters.name: playlist_id
parameters.description: Return a playlist's entries **in playing order** (ADR 0030). The only listing that may repeat an item id, which is why a playlist is keyed on position rather than on id.

parameters.name: genre
parameters.description: Restrict to items carrying this exact genre name. **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: decade
parameters.description: Restrict to a decade — `1990` means 1990–1999. A non-numeric value is `400`. **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: content_rating
parameters.description: Restrict to this exact content rating (PG, R, TV-MA…). **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: year
parameters.description: Restrict to this exact release year. A non-numeric value is `400`. **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: resolution
parameters.description: Restrict to a resolution tier — `uhd`, `hd1080`, `hd720`, `sd`. An **unrecognised key is ignored rather than rejected**: these arrive from bookmarked query strings, and a renamed tier should widen the grid back rather than break the page. **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: person
parameters.description: Restrict to items this person is credited on, **in any role**. Ids come from the library's cast list, and a non-numeric value is `400` — an id is machine-generated, so a malformed one means the caller is confused, and widening to the whole library would look like the person matched everything. **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: actor
parameters.description: The person filter scoped to acting credits. "Who is in this" and "who made this" are different questions, and `person` answers both without saying which was meant. Somebody who does both matches under both, once in each. **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: director
parameters.description: The person filter scoped to directing credits. **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: collection
parameters.description: Restrict to members of a collection. Reads the membership table, not `parent_id` — a film belongs to a franchise without being inside it (ADR 0017). **Repeatable.** Repeatable filters are OR within a facet and AND across facets: two genres widen the grid, adding a decade narrows it. A blank value is dropped rather than treated as a filter for the empty string.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: `in_progress` (started, not finished) or `unmatched` (no provider claimed it). **Single-valued**, because the two cannot usefully be combined.

parameters.name: min_rating
parameters.description:
Rated at least this highly, out of ten.

**Unrated items are excluded, not sunk.** A film with no rating is not a film rated zero, and sweeping them to the bottom would quietly hide the unmatched half of a library behind a control that says nothing about matching. An unparseable value widens rather than `400`s.

parameters.name: watched
parameters.description: `watched=false` restricts to items the calling user has not finished; any other value is ignored. Keys off the leaf's own play state, so it filters movies and episodes — a container carries no watched flag and is unaffected.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description:
`title` (default), `year`, `added`, `rating` (highest first, unrated last), or `track` (disc then track number).

**A container's children are not automatically in hierarchy order.** Episodes come back in season order only because they share their series' sort title and therefore tie, letting the order fall through. Tracks keep their own titles, so an album asked for without a sort comes back alphabetically — use `sort=track`.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Page size. Defaults to 100, maximum 500.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Page offset.

200.description: A page of items, plus the total before paging.

get.summary: One item, with the detail-only fields
get.description:
The list shape plus `genres`, `credits`, `artwork`, `locked_fields`, `ratings`, `streams` and `file_name`.

An item flagged `missing` still returns `200` with `"missing": true`, so the UI can explain the situation rather than pretend the item was never there.

200.description: The item, including a missing one.

put.description:
Clients should throttle to roughly one call per five seconds during playback.

Progress is per account (ADR 0006).

get.summary: In-progress items, most recently played first
get.description:
The home screen's first shelf.

**A show appears as the show, not as an episode.** Episodes collapse to the show they belong to, and `next_episode` carries the one the show would play — the same answer `GET /api/items/{id}/continue` gives, computed by the same query, so the shelf and a show's Continue button cannot disagree.

A show qualifies on **any** episode activity, watched or in progress. Finishing an episode is the ordinary way to stop watching a series, and a shelf that dropped the show at that moment answered "which episode did I stop inside" rather than "what am I watching". A show with every episode watched has nothing to continue and is absent.

For everything else — films, tracks — "in progress" is a saved position past zero with `watched` unset, so an item played to the end drops off rather than inviting a replay.

Progress and artwork are included so a tile draws its bar and poster without a second call.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Defaults to 20, maximum 100.

200.description: The shelf.

get.summary: How this file would be delivered, and why
get.description:
**Call it with the parameters you intend to stream with.** An explanation of a decision the server would not actually make sends you looking in the wrong place.

Two rules apply on top of whatever the profile allows, and both are about what happens *after* the decision rather than what the client can decode:

- **10-bit H.264 is never direct-played.** The codec name matches and browsers advertise H.264 support, but High 10 is outside every browser's baseline. Detected from `pix_fmt` where the probe reports one. HEVC, VP9 and AV1 carry 10-bit fine and are not penalised.
- **A stream is only copied if MP4 can carry it.** Every non-direct path rewraps into fragmented MP4, and "the client decodes this codec" is not the same claim as "MP4 holds it". VP8, Vorbis, FLAC and Opus are re-encoded rather than copied even when the profile allows them — ffmpeg refuses to start on an impossible mux, which surfaces as a dead player with no reason.

200.description: The decision, and the profile it was made under.

400.description: `audio` named a track that does not exist.

get.summary: The original file, as an attachment
get.description:
Same bytes as `GET /api/stream/{id}`, different intent. A stream is for a player and every browser treats it as one; this carries `Content-Disposition: attachment` with a filename built from the item's **metadata** rather than from its path — `Arrival (2016).mkv`, or `Storm of the Century - S02E07 - Pilot.mkv` for an episode, because `Pilot.mkv` collides with every other pilot ever made. The name is given in both the quoted `filename=` form and the RFC 5987 `filename*=UTF-8''` form, so a title outside ASCII survives.

**Never transcoded.** The transcoder exists so a device that cannot play a file can still watch it; a download that quietly returned a re-encoded copy would be a lie about what you have, and the one operation where the original matters most is the one that takes it off the server.

Range requests are honoured, so an interrupted transfer resumes — which is the case a nine-gigabyte file is in.

200.description: The file.

Content-Disposition.description: `attachment`, with the metadata-derived filename in both forms.

404.description: No file, or its path does not resolve inside the location it was scanned under. Containment is re-verified on every request that turns a database row into a filesystem path.

503.description: The file is missing from disk.

get.summary: The media file, direct play only
get.description:
Bytes served as stored, with range support. **`Range` is what makes seeking work, and it is the first thing to test when playback misbehaves.**

Files a client cannot play use the transcode endpoints, chosen by the client after consulting `/playback`.

200.description: The file.

503.description: The file is gone from disk.

get.summary: A progressive fragmented MP4, produced on demand
get.description:
Plays in any browser with no client library — the file path deliberately touches no third-party player (ADR 0013, amended by ADR 0050).

`Accept-Ranges: none`: a live transcode has no length and cannot be range-served, since bytes do not exist until ffmpeg produces them. Seeking forward restarts the stream from a new `t`.

**A client must render the refusals.** Both `409` and `429` are handed to a `<video>` element as a failed request, which the element reports as a bare `error` with no status and nothing to display — so a player that does not act on them shows a spinner for ever, which is indistinguishable from converting slowly. Retrying is not a recovery: the same request under a narrower profile is the same request.

200.description: The converted stream. `audio/mp4` when the decision is audio-only.

400.description: `audio` named a track that does not exist.

409.description: The file can be played directly, so transcoding it would be wasted CPU. Use `/api/stream/{id}`.

429.description: Past the concurrent-transcode limit. Logged with how many sessions are running against the ceiling, since that number is what separates "the limit is working" from "sessions are leaking".

get.summary: The same transcode as an HLS playlist with fMP4 segments
get.description:
For clients that speak HLS natively. Segment URLs point back at `GET /api/stream/{id}/hls/{session}/{name}`.

**This is not the hls.js path.** hls.js is vendored for live channels only, behind a setting that is off by default; the file path does not touch it.

200.description: The playlist.

parameters.name: session
parameters.description: The session id from the playlist.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The segment or init-segment filename from the playlist.

get.summary: One HLS segment
get.description: Clients follow these from the playlist rather than constructing them.

200.description: The segment.

get.summary: Running transcode sessions, and whether ffmpeg is available

200.description: Sessions and the selected encoder.

get.summary: Background probing progress

200.description: Progress, and whether ffprobe is installed at all.

post.summary: Queue already-probed items to be probed again
post.description:
Administrators only.

Needed because a probe is only as good as the build that made it. The pending queue is "never probed", so when the prober learns to record a field the decision engine depends on, every item probed by an older build keeps a decision made without it and nothing revisits them.

Stream rows are kept while an item is queued. Deleting them would widen the window in which an item has no codec information at all and every playback decision for it falls back to direct play.

**Pick the scope by what you are trying to correct, not by cost.** `incomplete` is defined by one technical criterion — a video stream stored without `pix_fmt` — and on a library where every file has one it matches **nothing** and answers `{"queued": 0}`. That is a correct answer to a different question, and it has been read as "everything is already up to date" by somebody re-probing to fix stored durations. Use `scope=all` with `library` for a library whose stored *values* are wrong.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description:
`incomplete` (default) re-probes only items a current build would learn something from — today, video streams stored without `pix_fmt`. This is the narrow, cheap option and the one to reach for.

`all` re-probes everything, optionally narrowed with `library`. Re-probing a large library is hours of ffprobe, which is why it has to be asked for by name and is never something the server decides to do on its own.

parameters.name: library
parameters.description: Narrow `scope=all` to one library.

200.description: How many were queued.

get.summary: Who the caller is, what they have watched, and the totals behind it
get.description: **The caller's own profile only.** There is no per-user variant of this route: "what has everyone been watching" needs an answer to who may see it before it needs a route.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: History page size. Defaults to 50, maximum 200.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: History page offset.

200.description: The caller's profile.

patch.description: The account **id does not change**, which is what makes this a rename rather than a replacement: sessions, watch history, ratings and playlist membership all hang off the id and follow silently.

200.description: The renamed account.

409.description: `duplicate` if the name is taken, or `no_account` on an unconfigured loopback server where there is no account to edit.

get.summary: How many playback records a reset would remove
get.description: **Removes nothing.** It exists so the confirmation can name a number: a person who expected to clear one show and is told four hundred has learned something while it is still free, and a number is what makes an irreversible action reviewable rather than a shrug.

200.description: The count, and the scope it was counted under.

delete.description:
**The account is the session's and there is no user id to supply.** Playback state is keyed by user (ADR 0006) so that one person's viewing is their own, and an administrator clearing their own history must not be able to reach into anybody else's — so the endpoint offers no way to name a victim. Running the server is not consent on somebody else's behalf.

Audited (ADR 0026): destructive and irreversible puts it in the same class as removing a library. The entry records the scope and the count, not the rows — "forgot 412 finished items" is what answers the question a month later, and a list of ids for things that may since have been deleted is not.

200.description: How many were removed.

get.summary: Everything you have rated, most recent first
get.description: Your list. There is no route to anybody else's.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Defaults to 50, maximum 200.

200.description: Your ratings, with the items they are about.

put.summary: Whether your activity is visible to other accounts
put.description:
The caller's own decision, and only ever the caller's. **There is deliberately no administrator variant**: an administrator may run the server, but a switch somebody else can flip on your behalf is not consent. Audited, because it changes who can see something about a person.

Turning it off is **retroactive**: past activity stops being visible along with future. A switch that cannot take back what it gave is not a switch.

Read the current value from `user.sharing` on `GET /api/auth/status`, **not** from `GET /api/people` — that list excludes the caller by design, so reading your own setting from it always answers undefined.

200.description: Acknowledged.

put.summary: Whether your account appears in the roster handed to paired servers
put.description:
Choosing to appear in a roster is one account's own decision about itself, and there is deliberately no admin-facing version of it — the same reasoning as the sharing switch. Pairing a server is administrative because it opens a network relationship for the whole server; being listed in one is not.

Read the current value from `user.visible_to_peers` on `GET /api/auth/status`.

200.description: Acknowledged.

get.summary: Your rating of an item
get.description: **These routes carry no user id**: whose rating is always the caller's, which makes it impossible to leak one by forgetting a filter.

200.description: Your rating, or null.
The rating as it now stands.

delete.description: **Not the same as scoring something 1.** "I have not rated this" and "I rated this badly" are different statements, and an interface that cannot say the first is one people stop trusting with the second.

get.summary: Server settings

200.description: The current settings, with provider keys reported only as configured flags.

put.description: Administrators only. Returns the settings as `GET` would.

200.description: The settings as they now stand.

post.summary: Restore the documented defaults
post.description:
Administrators only. Returns the settings, like `GET`.

**Credentials and machine facts survive**: the password hash, the provider API keys, the TLS certificate paths, and the ffmpeg directory. Wiping the first would lock the operator out of their own server and wiping the others would break metadata and HTTPS — none of which is what anybody means by "reset settings", and none of which a reset can restore. What resets is behaviour.

200.description: The settings, back at their defaults.

get.summary: List directories, for a folder picker
get.description:
Administrators only. Omit `path` to get the roots — drive letters on Windows, `/` elsewhere.

This discloses filesystem layout, which is why it is admin-gated. It grants no capability `POST /api/libraries` did not already have — that endpoint accepts and scans any path — but it makes enumeration convenient.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: The directory to list. Omit for the roots.

200.description: The directory's subdirectories.

400.description: The path could not be resolved.

post.summary: Start a scan of every library
post.description:
Administrators only. **Always `202`, never `409`** — unlike the single-library form, where the caller named one library and a conflict is the whole answer. Here the body says which libraries did what.

A library is also scanned automatically when it is created, so this is for "check everything for new media" rather than for setup.

202.description: What started, and what was already running.

get.summary: Live scan progress

200.description: Progress, whether or not a scan is running.

post.summary: Start an asynchronous scan
post.description:
Administrators only. Returns `202` immediately. **Scans are never queued.**

`kind` is permanent and there is no endpoint to change it: it decides which files are scanned at all — a `music` library indexes audio, a `picture` library images, everything else video — and it biases matching between films and TV. Altering it would mean a rescan re-litigating identity for an entire library, which is what field locking exists to prevent. Remove the library and add it again.

409.description:
A scan is already running — and the body is **the running scan's progress, in the same shape as the `202`**, not the error envelope every other failure uses.

That is deliberate and worth stating plainly, because a client parsing it as an error finds no `code` and no `message`: the useful answer to "start a scan" when one is already going is *how far that one has got*, and this endpoint gives it. **Branch on the status, not on the body.**

get.summary: The filter values this library's browse view offers

200.description: Only values actually present.

get.summary: The people credited in one library
get.description:
A search endpoint rather than another array on `/facets`, because the two differ by three orders of magnitude: a library has a dozen genres and thousands of credited people, and shipping all of them on every browse load would be a megabyte of JSON populating a control most visits never open.

Ordered by how much of the library each person is in, then by name — **a total order**, so a list re-fetched as you type cannot appear to shuffle itself.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Prefix-or-word match, so `vance` finds Ada Vance and `ada v` finds her too.

parameters.name: role
parameters.description: Scopes the search to one side of the camera (`actor`, `director`). **Unvalidated on purpose**: an unknown role matches nobody and returns an empty list, which is the truthful answer — rejecting it would turn a filter nobody can satisfy into an error page.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description:
**Repeatable**, and resolves specific people *instead of* searching — which is what lets a filter pill render a name. Filter state lives in the URL, so a bookmarked `?person=12` arrives with an id and nothing else, and a pill reading "person 12" is not a filter anybody can read.

Answers in the order asked for, so pills do not reorder between reloads; an id with no row is skipped rather than returned blank.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Defaults to 50, maximum 200.

200.description: Matching people.

get.summary: What this library's people have been playing lately

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Defaults to 12, maximum 50.

200.description: Ranked titles, with the scale to read them at.

get.summary: A picture library's photographs counted by capture month
get.description:
Open a bucket through the ordinary item listing:

- `GET /api/items?library_id=5&kind=photo&sort=taken&taken_month=2019-07`
- `GET /api/items?library_id=5&kind=photo&sort=taken&taken_undated=1`

Either parameter also excludes marked folders, so a listing always agrees with the count above it.

200.description: Buckets, newest first, with `undated` last.

**Distinct from `refresh`, and the distinction is the point.** Refresh asks the provider the same question again; this corrects the question. A film whose year lived only in its folder name was searched with no year at all, and no number of refreshes would have changed that answer.

Scope is deliberately narrow: only `review` and `unmatched` rows are touched (a `matched` row's title came from a provider, which is better evidence than any filename); `locked` and `local` rows are never offered; field locks are honoured **individually**, so an item whose title a person corrected still has its year re-parsed; and an empty guess never clears a populated field.
